The paper was published in a mid-2010s issue of a monthly peer-reviewed chemistry journal established in 2009, and it demonstrates autonomous healing at sub-zero temperatures and has over 1,400 citations. question: Back in the early 20th century, a stuffed toy bear named after a US president was invented by a Russian immigrant couple in Brooklyn. This bear was produced by a company that later became America's largest doll maker, which also manufactured a popular drink-and-wet doll in the 1930s. Decades later, this same company manufactured a historically significant doll that featured a head sculpted by a sculptor who created multiple molds to achieve an authentic chestnut brown complexion. That doll was created by a businesswoman from a southern state after observing African American children playing with white dolls in the late 1940s. The creation of this doll was influenced by a psychological study conducted in the late 1930s that surveyed a group of African American preschool children in the nation's capital to examine racial identity through doll preference experiments. That study was the master's thesis of a psychologist who co-founded the first full-time psychological services institution in a predominantly African American neighborhood in New York City, which she directed for over three decades. Her research also demonstrated that Black children became aware of their racial identity at about age three and acquired a negative self-image, findings that were completed roughly a decade and a half before a landmark Supreme Court ruling that ended school segregation. The toy company was later sold to a media conglomerate's toy division at the beginning of the 1980s for a sum in the tens of millions. What is the name of the psychologist who conducted that master's thesis?
exact_answer: Mamie Phipps Clark

The selling organization also maintains a near‑perfect customer rating from several hundred reviews on a major online marketplace, and issues a signed document after each artifact undergoes inspection by team members professionally trained in counterfeit detection. question: Back in the early 1970s, a weekly news magazine founded in 1923—which remained a weekly for nearly a century before switching to biweekly in 2020—published an investigative piece that exposed a literary fraud. The billionaire also married a Houston socialite in the mid-1920s but divorced shortly after due to his obsession with film production, and he became increasingly reclusive, acquiring multiple properties in a major Nevada gambling destination. question: Back in the early 1960s, an international award for science popularization—established in the early 1950s through an Indian donation—was given to a publisher who, in the mid‑20th century, had purchased a well‑known science magazine along with partners. This publisher later authored a comprehensive history of 20th‑century scientific discoveries in the early 2000s, led the world’s largest general scientific society (founded in the mid‑19th century) during the mid‑1980s, and was married in the mid‑1950s to a prominent civil rights attorney. The magazine he purchased was founded in the mid‑1800s in a major East Coast city by a person known for his inventions, and it is now owned by an academic publishing company formed in 2015 through a merger, generating nearly $30 million in revenue with about 240 employees. In the early 1960s, this magazine published a paper authored by an American researcher known for rodent studies on crowding effects. The paper introduced a concept that was demonstrated by a multi‑year late‑1960s mouse experiment that peaked at several thousand subjects before collapsing despite adequate resources. That concept emerged from research conducted in a suburban city in the Washington metropolitan area, where early experiments involved dozens of rodents in small confined spaces. The concept was later challenged by a psychologist’s 1975 human behavior study that found no significant negative effects from crowding. The paper itself documented that populations of over 80 animals exhibited severe behavioral abnormalities in confined spaces, with infant mortality rates exceeding 90% in the most disoriented groups. What is the name of this paper?

He also received academic backing from Claude Lévi-Strauss, leading to a university appointment in the mid-1960s. The analyst wrote a letter as one of seven foundational texts about psychoanalytic institutional structures. This letter, written in the mid-1960s, formally announced the dissolution of a psychoanalytic school that had been founded in the mid-1960s following its exclusion from another organization due to conflicts with a global professional organization founded in the early 1910s over training practices. This training concept implements a unique structure with supervised "fourth analyses" and rejects charismatic authority, emphasizing clinical autonomy. The splinter organization publishes an annual publication series and developed a concept for understanding psychosis. The school that was dissolved was actually dissolved in the early 1980s, leading to the formation of a new organization by its founder. question:
Consider the world's most extensive astronomical glass plate collection, containing over 550,000 negatives documenting over 150 years of observations. This collection is housed at an organization that also employed over 146 women astronomical computers from the 1880s to the 1960s, who studied these plates and made significant discoveries. The collection itself was the subject of a two-decade digitization effort led by a professor who holds the Robert Treat Paine Professor of Practical Astronomy title, completing in the early 2020s after scanning over 450,000 plates. Its founding was funded by a 19th-century woman astronomer who established a memorial fund in 1886, creating the Henry Draper Memorial as its core. The collection also features contemporary artistic interpretations, including works by an associate professor of art studio at a women's college who created monuments honoring historical women astronomers. The organization maintains modern research initiatives: a searchable digital platform connecting over 428,000 plates with more than 2,500 notebooks created by pioneering women scientists, and a project focusing on historical notebooks. This project utilizes crowdsourcing through a platform started in 2013 that has engaged over 56,000 volunteers for transcription work, and employs a global citizen science platform with over a million volunteers to identify non-textual items through its "Star Notes" initiative, which completed Phase 1 in mid-2022. The project makes its transcriptions searchable on a system operated by a research institute founded in 1890 under a NASA cooperative agreement. This system maintains three bibliographic databases containing more than 13 million records covering astronomy, physics, and arXiv e-prints, and is expanding beyond its original focus to include additional science domains under an initiative per NASA request.

Now, an astronomer from this organization authored a paper documenting a celestial object with a perfect halo of approximately 17 arc seconds in radius surrounding a central image. This discovery was published in a peer-reviewed monthly publication founded in 1849 and owned by the American Astronomical Society since 1941, in the mid-20th century. In that paper, the author considered a gravitational lensing scenario and calculated a specific mass for the central object. What was that calculated mass?

The participation of these other creditors was part of a restructuring transaction announced in mid‑December 2021 with an expected completion by March 15. Additionally, the presentation showed that quarterly trading volumes declined significantly from over 13 million tonnes to around 8 million tonnes between Q3 and Q4 of the reporting period. What is the exact name of this financial report?

Now, this technology service hosts, as a PDF file published in the early 2010s, a financial report filed as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit by a San Francisco–based international nonprofit that connects people through crowdfunded loans to alleviate poverty worldwide. The report contains multiple parts including sections for governance, compliance, and financial reporting with revenue around several million dollars. According to this document's description, what was the loan repayment rate achieved by the nonprofit during that year?

question: Consider a bacterium that was selected as the preferred host organism for recombinant DNA production at the 1975 Asilomar Conference. It was later the subject of a historical analysis by a Ph.D. historian, published around 2007 in the Food and Drug Law Institute's bimonthly publication, and also featured in a 2023 genomic study of its ancestral progenitor strains—one still carrying bacteriophage lambda and the F plasmid, the other sequenced alongside strain WG1. Additionally, in 2023, the same bacterium was the subject of a research paper in a Gold Open Access journal from the Microbiology Society, co-authored by a molecular biologist at a UK university. This bacterium was used to manufacture the first commercial recombinant DNA product, approved under NDA 18-790 in the early 1980s through a dual-chain fermentation process. The product was introduced by a pharmaceutical company. That same company conducted a major clinical trial in the early 2020s, registered under NCT03730662, which enrolled over 2,000 participants across more than a dozen countries with treatment duration exceeding 80 weeks. The trial demonstrated that a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist slowed the decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate by approximately 2.2 mL/min per 1.73 m² per year compared to a standard insulin therapy. The kidney outcomes of this trial were later presented at a diabetes conference in New Orleans. A post-hoc analysis of these kidney outcomes was published in Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology with first author Hiddo J L Heerspink. The primary trial paper, funded by the same company, reported these findings. What is its title?

The musician also collaborated with others across multiple continents to deepen their understanding of specialized tuning systems, culminating in the release of a custom replica instrument. That replica was built on a large-bodied Japanese acoustic guitar from the late 1970s, unlike the original smaller parlor guitar, and underwent several enhancement phases from the mid-2010s to early 2020s with additional frets added. Its structural modifications and fretwork were performed by an experienced Australian luthier in a regional city, with financial backing from an ensemble known for multi-year artistic initiatives. Separately, a clone of a classic dreadnought guitar model—fitted with an award-winning bridge plate pickup and using specially coated strings—can be heard on a 2024 album.
